newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian port broods on policeman's death.
newsitem.headline: Albanian port broods on policeman's death.

text.p: The body of Ali Shika was carried on Sunday through the streets of Durres by Albanian police weeping openly at the death of their comrade.
"This man never hurt anyone and now he is dead," said one of his comrades. "Where is the justice in that?"
Automobiles pulled to the curb and pedestrians in this port city fell silent as the funeral procession passed.
Some secret police in civilian clothes got out of their cars carrying Kalashnikovs and joined the mourners on foot.
"May God cut the hands off the man who did this," said an elderly woman standing on the sidewalk as the body passed.
Ali Shika was 30 when he was killed on Saturday afternoon. Police said he had stopped a vehicle and asked to search it when the driver pulled out a gun and shot him.
The sight of a dead policeman borne on an army stretcher caused the residents of this city to pause and reflect about the future of their city and their country.

Despite the unrest in Albania following the collapse of five pyramid schemes, which wiped out the life-savings of tens of thousands of families, Durres remained firmly under government control until Thursday.
That day the country's largest port teetered on the verge of anarchy as shooting and looting erupted in parts of the city. Since then the police have regained control.

Residents have been given a second chance to ask themselves if they want to go the way of southern Albania, where police and army units have collapsed or withdrawn and local citizens' committees share control with clan-based mafia organisations.

Ali Shika's procession, grown to about 100 strong, halted in a square by the city's main mosque and in front of its main administrative building. Scores of city workers watched impassively from the building's windows and front steps.

The police formed up and fired a thunderous volley into the air from their Kalashnikovs as a salute to their dead colleague -- a gesture that made up in noise what it lacked in finesse. Empty shell casings rained down like brass confetti.
One policeman shouted to the city workers: "Don't stand there watching us. Get out here. This man died for you too."
Sheepishly, those on the steps walked over, warily eyeing the police and their guns.
The crowd moved across the square to the steps of the Mayor's office where policemen, many choking with tears, praised the dead man and cursed the mafia they say killed him.
"We are the police and we do not need anyone to join us," one of the men declared from the steps. "We will save the city and destroy the mafia."

Murmurs swept through the crowd of several hundred townspeople now standing on the plaza at the bottom of the steps. One civilian blared out: "Long live the police, long live Durres" and began applauding the officers.
The crowd joined in and then the police begin applauding as well and finally the procession wound away through the dusty streets.
